stories.event: He went to study for twelve years after his wedding.
stories.turn: On his return his wife had become infertile, and divorce or a second wife would both shame her.
stories.outcome: He prayed for her and she was cured.
stories.summary: Rabbi's son left to study for twelve years and came back to find his wife infertile. Rabbi saw that divorcing her or taking a second wife would both humiliate her, so the husband prayed for mercy and she was healed.

stories.event: He left for the study hall without waiting for Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai and studied for twelve years.
stories.turn: On returning he could not find his home; when his wife saw him she died from shock.
stories.outcome: He prayed for her and she was revived.
stories.summary: Hananya ben Hakhinai went off to study for twelve years. When he returned the town had changed; he found his house by following a girl called 'daughter of Hakhinai'. His wife saw him suddenly and died of shock, and after he protested to God and prayed, she lived.

stories.event: After twelve years of study he went to the local study hall first and sent word home.
stories.turn: He met a brilliant young scholar, not realizing it was his own son, and later stood up for him at home.
stories.outcome: His wife pointed out that a father was standing for his son.
stories.summary: Hama bar Bisa, wishing to avoid Ben Hakhinai's mistake, sent word home before arriving. In the study hall he was impressed by a sharp young man and regretted not having such a son; at home he rose for the same young man, and his wife told him it was his son Oshaya.

stories.actor: Rabbi Akiva and Ben Kalba Savua's daughter
stories.event: She betrothed herself to the shepherd Akiva on condition he study, and her father disinherited her.
stories.turn: Akiva returned after twenty-four years with thousands of students, honored his wife, and her father came to annul his vow.
stories.outcome: Akiva revealed himself; the father kissed his feet and gave him half his wealth.
stories.summary: Ben Kalba Savua's daughter married the shepherd Akiva secretly and sent him to study, and her father cast her out. Akiva studied twelve years, overheard her urging another twelve, and returned with 24,000 students; he defended her when his attendants pushed her away. Her father came to the great sage to annul his vow, learned the sage was Akiva, and gave him half his property.

stories.event: Wishing to give away his movable property, he was told it must be transferred by means of land.
stories.turn: He bought a small plot near Jerusalem and gave the property along with portions of it.
stories.outcome: He died and the Sages carried out his gift.
stories.summary: A Madonite in Jerusalem wanted to give away his many movables and was told he could only do so through land. He acquired a plot, gave its northern part with a hundred sheep and a hundred barrels, then died, and the Sages upheld his gift.

stories.event: He wanted to give his movables as a gift and was told to do it through land.
stories.turn: He bought a small plot and gave a handbreadth of it with sheep and barrels.
stories.outcome: He died and the Sages fulfilled his words.
stories.summary: A man in Jerusalem, sick or healthy depending on the version, wished to give away his movable property. Told it had to go through land, he bought a beit rova and gave a square handbreadth with a hundred sheep and barrels. He died and the Sages carried out his instructions.

stories.event: Ulla, who often went up to Eretz Yisrael, died abroad.
stories.turn: Told his coffin was being brought to the Land, Rabbi Elazar said burial after death is not like being received alive.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Elazar lamented him despite the coffin's return.
stories.summary: Ulla died outside Eretz Yisrael and Rabbi Elazar lamented that he died in an unclean land. When told his coffin was coming, he replied that being absorbed by the Land in life is not like after death.

stories.actor: A man with a yevama in Bei Hoza'a
stories.event: He asked Rabbi Hanina whether he could go down to Babylonia to perform levirate marriage.
stories.turn: Rabbi Hanina said his brother had left and died for it.
stories.outcome: He told him not to follow his brother out of the Land.
stories.summary: A man in Eretz Yisrael whose brother's widow lived in Babylonia asked Rabbi Hanina whether he could go there to marry her. Rabbi Hanina answered that his brother had married abroad and God killed him, so why should he follow?

stories.actor: A man who left Pumbedita for Bei Kuvei
stories.event: He moved from Pumbedita to Bei Kuvei.
stories.turn: Rav Yosef held this forbidden.
stories.outcome: Rav Yosef excommunicated him.
stories.summary: A man left Pumbedita to live in Bei Kuvei, beyond Babylonia proper, and Rav Yosef excommunicated him.

stories.actor: A scholar who left Pumbedita for Astonia
stories.event: He moved from Pumbedita to Astonia.
stories.turn: He died there.
stories.outcome: Abaye said he would have lived had he stayed.
stories.summary: A Torah scholar left Pumbedita for Astonia and died. Abaye remarked that had he wished to stay in Babylonia he would still be alive.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and Rabbi Hiyya
stories.event: Rabbi Hiyya visited the ill Rabbi and found him crying.
stories.turn: Hiyya reminded him that dying in tears is a bad sign.
stories.outcome: Rabbi explained he was crying for the Torah and mitzvot he would lose.
stories.summary: When Rabbi fell ill, Rabbi Hiyya came in and found him weeping, and asked why, since crying at death is an ill omen. Rabbi answered that he wept for the Torah and commandments he could no longer fulfill.

stories.event: During an argument Hanina boasted he could restore the Torah by his analysis if it were forgotten.
stories.turn: Hiyya answered that he works so it will never be forgotten.
stories.outcome: Hiyya described planting flax, hunting deer, making scrolls and teaching children who teach each other.
stories.summary: Arguing with Rabbi Hiyya, Rabbi Hanina claimed he could rebuild a forgotten Torah through his reasoning. Hiyya replied that he ensures it is never forgotten: he grows flax for nets, traps deer, feeds orphans the meat, writes scrolls on the hides, and teaches each child one book or order to pass on to the others.

stories.actor: Rav Nahman's relative and her daughter
stories.event: A relative of Rav Nahman sold her ketuba rights, was divorced and died, and the buyers claimed it from her daughter.
stories.turn: Rav Nahman hinted aloud that the daughter could forgive the ketuba to her father and inherit it from him.
stories.outcome: She did so, and Rav Nahman later regretted acting like an advocate.
stories.summary: Rav Nahman's relative sold her marriage contract rights, then was divorced and died, and the buyers came to collect from her daughter. Rav Nahman remarked that someone should advise her to forgive the debt to her father and inherit it from him later; she heard and did so. Rav Nahman afterwards said he had made himself like a judge's advocate.

stories.actor: An Amorite and a resident of Eretz Yisrael
stories.event: The Amorite asked how much the palm by the Jordan yielded and heard sixty kor.
stories.turn: He mocked that they had ruined the land, since it once gave 120.
stories.outcome: The resident replied he meant one side only.
stories.summary: An Amorite asked an Israelite how many dates they harvested from a palm on the Jordan. Told sixty kor, he scoffed that they had already ruined the land, since his people took 120. The Israelite answered that he had counted only one side of the tree.

stories.event: He ascended to Eretz Yisrael, was ordained, and was appointed to the calendar council.
stories.turn: At each step he declared himself spared another curse.
stories.outcome: He escaped all three curses of the false prophets.
stories.summary: On arriving in Eretz Yisrael Rabbi Elazar said he was spared one curse, on ordination two, and on joining the intercalation council three.

stories.event: Going up to Eretz Yisrael he found no ferry and crossed the Jordan by a rope.
stories.turn: A Sadducee mocked the Jews as hasty.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Zeira answered that he hurried lest he lose a privilege denied Moses and Aaron.
stories.summary: Rabbi Zeira, finding no ferry, pulled himself across the Jordan on a rope. A Sadducee called the Jews a rash people, and Zeira replied that he could not be sure he would merit a land Moses and Aaron never entered.

stories.actor: A millstone owner and his renter
stories.event: A man rented a millstone in exchange for grinding services.
stories.turn: The owner grew rich, bought his own mill and donkey, and demanded money instead.
stories.outcome: The renter refused, saying he agreed only to grind.
stories.summary: A man rented out his millstone in return for grinding his grain. Once rich, he bought his own mill and demanded payment in money, but the renter insisted he had only agreed to grind for him.

stories.actor: Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi and a couple
stories.event: A groom complained he found no blood and the bride said she was a virgin.
stories.turn: Rabban Gamliel tested two maidservants on a wine barrel and then the bride.
stories.outcome: The wine scent did not pass through her, and he told the groom to take his acquisition.
stories.summary: A groom came to Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi saying he found no blood; the bride insisted she was a virgin. Gamliel seated a virgin and non-virgin maidservant on a wine barrel to test the method, then the bride, whose breath carried no wine scent, and ruled her a virgin.

stories.actor: Rabban Gamliel the Elder and a couple
stories.event: A groom found no blood and the bride said she was of the Dorketi family, who have none.
stories.turn: Rabban Gamliel investigated her relatives and found it true.
stories.outcome: He told the groom to take his acquisition and called him fortunate.
stories.summary: A groom complained to Rabban Gamliel the Elder that he found no blood. The bride said her family, the Dorketi, have neither menstrual nor hymeneal blood; Gamliel checked her relatives, confirmed it, and told the groom to keep her.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and a couple
stories.event: A groom found no blood and the bride said she was a virgin, during a famine.
stories.turn: Rabbi saw their faces were black with hunger and had them bathed and fed.
stories.outcome: The groom then found blood, and Rabbi told him to take his acquisition.
stories.summary: During years of drought a groom told Rabbi he found no blood while the bride maintained her virginity. Noticing they were starved, Rabbi had them bathed, fed and sent to a room; the groom then found blood, and Rabbi quoted a verse about skin shriveled on bones.

stories.actor: Rabbi Zeira and Rava in Mehoza
stories.event: Rabbi Zeira taught that a convert may marry a mamzeret and the converts pelted him with etrogim.
stories.turn: Rava taught that a convert may marry a priest's daughter and was carried on silk, then repeated the mamzeret ruling.
stories.outcome: When the people complained, Rava said he had given them both options.
stories.summary: Rabbi Zeira taught in Mehoza that a convert may marry a mamzeret, and the many converts there stoned him with etrogim. Rava then taught that a convert may marry a priest's daughter and was carried on silk, but later also taught the mamzeret ruling; to their protest he answered he had done them good, letting them marry from either group.

stories.event: They seized an orphans' cow for a debt and Rabbi Yohanan approved.
stories.turn: Reish Lakish told them to return it.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yohanan said he could do nothing, as his equal disagreed.
stories.summary: Rabbi Yohanan's relatives seized a cow belonging to orphans and he told them they had done well. Reish Lakish ordered them to give it back, and when they returned to Rabbi Yohanan he said he could not overrule a peer who disagreed with him.

stories.actor: An orphans' herdsman and a creditor
stories.event: A creditor seized an ox from the herdsman and claimed he took it before the debtor died.
stories.turn: The herdsman said it was after, and they went to Rav Nahman.
stories.outcome: With no witnesses to the seizure, Rav Nahman believed the creditor.
stories.summary: A creditor took an ox from the herdsman of some orphans, claiming he seized it while their father lived; the herdsman said it was after his death. Rav Nahman asked for witnesses to the seizure, and when there were none, ruled the creditor credible.

stories.actor: The house of the Nasi and the judges
stories.event: The Nasi's household seized an orphans' maidservant, and Rabbi Abbahu approved.
stories.turn: Rabbi Abba accused the judges of flattering the Nasi's house, citing Reish Lakish's reversal.
stories.outcome: The window ends with Rabbi Abba's rebuke.
stories.summary: Members of the Nasi's house seized a maidservant of orphans for a debt, and Rabbi Abbahu told them they had done well. Rabbi Abba challenged the judges for currying favor, recalling that Reish Lakish had reversed such a ruling.

stories.event: A son-in-law passed by his father-in-law's door.
stories.turn: There were rumors about him and his mother-in-law.
stories.outcome: Rav Sheshet had him flogged.
stories.summary: A son-in-law walked past his father-in-law's house, and because of rumors linking him with his mother-in-law, Rav Sheshet flogged him.

stories.actor: A man betrothing with a myrtle mat
stories.event: He betrothed a woman with a mat of myrtle.
stories.turn: Told it was worth less than a peruta, he said she should be betrothed with the four dinars inside it.
stories.outcome: She took it silently, and Rava ruled the silence meaningless.
stories.summary: A man betrothed a woman with a myrtle mat, and bystanders objected it was worthless. He declared she should be betrothed by the four dinars wrapped in it; she took it and said nothing, and Rava ruled that silence after the money is given counts for nothing.

stories.actor: Rav Hiyya bar Adda and Reish Lakish
stories.event: The children's teacher was absent for three days.
stories.turn: He explained he was harvesting an enormously fruitful vine, whose yield fell each day.
stories.outcome: Reish Lakish told him it would have yielded more had he not neglected the children.
stories.summary: Rav Hiyya bar Adda, a teacher, stayed away three days, and Reish Lakish asked why. He said he was harvesting a vine left by his father, three hundred clusters a day, yielding less wine each day; Reish Lakish answered that his absence from teaching was why the yield shrank.

stories.event: Visiting Benei Berak he saw goats under fig trees.
stories.turn: Honey dripped from the figs and milk from the goats and they mixed.
stories.outcome: He declared this the meaning of 'flowing with milk and honey'.
stories.summary: Rami bar Yehezkel came to Benei Berak and saw goats grazing under figs, with honey oozing from the fruit and milk dripping from the goats into it. He said this was what 'a land flowing with milk and honey' means.

stories.event: A man asked what the law is if one's mother is divorced.
stories.turn: Rabbi Yehoshua saw from his tears he was a widow's son.
stories.outcome: He answered sarcastically to pour water and call them like chickens.
stories.summary: A man asked Rabbi Yehoshua about honoring a divorced mother. Seeing from his tear-filled eyes that he was a widow's son, Rabbi Yehoshua mocked the question, telling him to pour water in a pitcher and cluck at his parents like chickens.

stories.event: The Sages wanted to buy merchandise from him at a huge profit.
stories.turn: The key lay under his sleeping father's head.
stories.outcome: He did not wake his father and lost the sale.
stories.summary: Asked how far honoring parents goes, Rav Ulla told of Dama ben Netina of Ashkelon, a gentile. The Sages offered a deal worth 600,000 dinars, but the key was under his sleeping father's head and he would not disturb him.

stories.event: He refused to wake his father to sell stones for the ephod.
stories.turn: The next year a red heifer was born in his herd.
stories.outcome: He asked the Sages only for the sum he had lost honoring his father.
stories.summary: Dama ben Netina gave up a sale of ephod stones rather than wake his father, who slept on the key. The following year God rewarded him with a red heifer; when the Sages came to buy it, he asked only for the money he had lost for his father's honor.

stories.actor: Dama ben Netina and his mother
stories.event: He sat in a gold cloak among the nobles of Rome.
stories.turn: His mother tore the cloak, struck his head and spat in his face.
stories.outcome: He did not shame her.
stories.summary: Once Dama ben Netina sat among Roman nobles in a golden cloak, and his mother came, tore it off, slapped him and spat at him. He did not humiliate her in return.

stories.event: A Divine Voice declared all present at Rabbi's funeral destined for the World-to-Come, but a launderer who visited Rabbi daily had missed it.
stories.turn: Hearing of Rabbi's death, he threw himself from a roof and died.
stories.outcome: A Divine Voice declared he too was destined for the World-to-Come.
stories.summary: On the day of Rabbi's funeral a heavenly voice promised the World-to-Come to all who attended. A launderer who came to Rabbi every day had not come that day; on hearing the news he climbed to a roof, fell and died, and a heavenly voice declared that he too would have a share.

stories.actor: Mar Zutra and Rabbi Yehuda of India
stories.event: Mar Zutra visited the dying convert who had no heirs.
stories.turn: Seeing death near, he had the convert's slave carry his shoes home to acquire him.
stories.outcome: The convert died and Mar Zutra gained the slave.
stories.summary: Rabbi Yehuda of India, a convert without heirs, fell ill and Mar Zutra visited him. Seeing he was about to die, Mar Zutra told his slave to take off his shoes and carry them to his house, acquiring him; one departed to death and the other to life.

stories.event: A man helped Shmuel off a ferry.
stories.turn: The man said he had a case before him.
stories.outcome: Shmuel disqualified himself.
stories.summary: As Shmuel crossed on a ferry a man gave him a hand. When the man said he had a case pending, Shmuel declared himself disqualified from judging it.

stories.event: While he judged, a man removed a feather from his head.
stories.turn: The man had a case before him.
stories.outcome: Ameimar disqualified himself.
stories.summary: A feather landed on Ameimar's head as he sat in judgment and a man brushed it off. Learning the man had a case, Ameimar disqualified himself.

stories.event: A man covered spittle lying before Mar Ukva.
stories.turn: The man had a case before him.
stories.outcome: Mar Ukva disqualified himself.
stories.summary: A man covered some spittle in front of Mar Ukva. When he said he had a case, Mar Ukva declared himself unfit to judge it.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei
stories.event: His sharecropper brought the weekly fruit basket early, on Thursday.
stories.turn: He had a case that day; Rabbi Yishmael refused the fruit and appointed other judges, yet found himself rooting for him.
stories.outcome: He cursed bribe-takers, reasoning that real bribes must bias far more.
stories.summary: Rabbi Yishmael's sharecropper brought his fruit on Thursday instead of Friday because he had a case. Rabbi Yishmael refused the basket, disqualified himself and seated two other scholars, but caught himself thinking of arguments for the man. He exclaimed that if he who took nothing felt this, those who take bribes are far worse.

stories.event: A man from afar brought him the first shearing.
stories.turn: He admitted he came because he had a case.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yishmael refused the gift and disqualified himself.
stories.summary: A man brought the priest Rabbi Yishmael bar Elisha the first shearing from a distant town. Asked why he passed other priests, he said he had a case before him, and Rabbi Yishmael refused the gift and the case.

stories.actor: A man and a woman washing her feet
stories.event: He grabbed coins from another man and threw them to her, declaring her betrothed.
stories.turn: The case came before Rava.
stories.outcome: Rava ruled the betrothal void, since the coins were stolen.
stories.summary: A man snatched dinars from someone and threw them to a woman washing her feet, saying she was betrothed. Rava ruled that nobody follows Rabbi Shimon's view that the owner despairs, so the betrothal was void.

stories.event: He betrothed a woman with a handful of onions from the field.
stories.turn: Rava asked who had permitted him to take them.
stories.outcome: The betrothal was invalid as stolen goods.
stories.summary: A sharecropper betrothed a woman with a handful of onions from the field he worked. Rava asked who had given them to him, implying they were stolen and the betrothal failed.

stories.event: He betrothed a woman with beer sediment belonging to his employer.
stories.turn: The owner found him and asked why he had not used the better sediment.
stories.outcome: Rava ruled that this does not imply consent outside teruma.
stories.summary: A brewer betrothed a woman with sediment from his employer's beer. The owner caught him and asked why he hadn't used the sharper sediment; Rava ruled that such a remark shows consent only regarding teruma, so the brewer had no right to it.

stories.event: He suffered for love of a woman and wanted to leave Eretz Yisrael.
stories.turn: He heard the teaching about the importance of the Land.
stories.outcome: He stayed and suffered until his death.
stories.summary: A man pining for a certain woman wanted to leave Eretz Yisrael. On hearing how important burial and life in the Land are, he stayed and endured his longing until the day he died.

stories.event: He arranged a match for his son with Rabbi Hiyya's family.
stories.turn: The bride died when the ketuba was being written.
stories.outcome: They examined lineage and found a difference in descent from David's line.
stories.summary: Rabbi arranged for his son to marry into Rabbi Hiyya's family, but the girl died as the marriage contract was being written. Fearing a flaw, they checked the families and found Rabbi descended from Shefatya son of Avital and Hiyya from Shimi, David's brother.

stories.event: Betrothed into Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra's family, he agreed to study twelve years before marrying.
stories.turn: After seeing the bride he cut it to six years, then married first, and was ashamed before his father.
stories.outcome: His father reassured him, then he studied twelve years; his wife became infertile and he prayed and she was cured.
stories.summary: Rabbi's son was to study twelve years before marrying a daughter of Yosei ben Zimra. Seeing her, he reduced it to six, then insisted on marrying first, and felt ashamed; Rabbi told him he had acted like God, who brought the Sanctuary forward. He then studied twelve years, returned to find her infertile, and prayed until she was healed.

stories.event: He left for twelve years of study without waiting for Rabbi Shimon.
stories.turn: Returning, he found home by following his daughter, and his wife died of shock.
stories.outcome: He prayed and she revived.
stories.summary: Hananya ben Hakhinai studied away for twelve years and on returning could not find his house. He followed a girl called 'daughter of Hakhinai' home; his wife saw him and died of shock, and he prayed and she lived.

stories.event: Returning after twelve years, he went to the study hall first and sent word home.
stories.turn: A sharp young scholar questioned him, and he regretted not having a son like that.
stories.outcome: The window ends with his regret.
stories.summary: Hama bar Bisa, avoiding Ben Hakhinai's mistake, waited in the local study hall after twelve years away. His own son Oshaya, unrecognized, came and debated with him, and Hama lamented that had he been home he would have had such a child.

stories.event: A mikveh in Yavne presumed full was measured and found deficient, raising the status of earlier purifications.
stories.turn: Tarfon ruled them pure and Akiva impure; they traded parables until Akiva's analysis prevailed.
stories.outcome: Tarfon conceded, saying whoever parts from Akiva parts from life.
stories.summary: A reservoir in Yavne thought to hold forty se'a was found short, and Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva disputed the purity of everything immersed in it. Each offered a parable about a disqualified priest; Akiva showed his comparison fit better, and Tarfon conceded with praise for him.
